requirements.requirement: On node1, only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs.
requirements.summary: The final state has an exact two-entry /etc/cron.allow containing root and opsadmin, owned by root:root with mode 0600. Both named accounts reach the permitted crontab path (reporting only that no crontab exists), while the unlisted nobody account is explicitly denied. The policy and active crond service persist across a verified reboot.

overall_summary: The cron access-control outcome is satisfied. The restart protocol is complete and coherent: node1 was healthy before restart, the restart was acknowledged, its boot ID changed from fbdf5b2c-bb43-49f6-935d-fb98f8a972f6 to 1d2d86bf-d186-4205-98be-152e75b53678, and the running system, crond service, allow-list, accounts, and access behavior recovered. Fixed lifecycle observations independently confirm the boot change.
limitations: No test crontab was actually installed; permission is demonstrated through the distinct crontab access-check messages and the exact allow-list rather than a schedule-and-execute test. This is strong evidence for access control but slightly lowers confidence.
Only one representative unlisted account was behaviorally tested, although the exact two-entry allow-list directly supports denial of all other users.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Creating opsadmin and the secured allow-list directly established the required outcome; restorecon ensured the policy file had an appropriate SELinux label; diagnostic temporary files were removed; and the reboot was required by the provider-wide evidence protocol. Post-executor observations show no failed services, new exposure, package damage, or abandoned temporary files. Boot-related PID and systemd-private-directory changes are expected consequences of the reboot.
